messages.subject: beanplots, axis, censored data
parts:
Hi there,

I'm fairly new to R and very new to ggplot2 (although I am avidly
reading the book in the evenings). I've got three questions which I
would appreciate help on.

1) Beanplots - I'm guessing that it's possible to reproduce these
plots using ggplot2, but I've no clue as to how. Has anybody
attempted it?

2) 2nd x axis. I understand and accept the limitation on 2nd axes as
enforced by ggplot2, but I am curious as to whether the location of
the x axis can be changed. I would like to plot how concentrations of
contaminants changes down a soil profile and it makes more sense (as
well as commonly accepted) to have an x axis on the top rather than
the bottom. Can this be done?

3) Censored data: How does one deal with this in ggplot2? I've been
using the NADA package which does a pretty good job, but I prefer the
aesthetics of ggplot2.

Sincerely,
Michael Hopgood

messages.subject: Re: beanplots, axis, censored data
parts:
> 1) Beanplots - I'm guessing that it's possible to reproduce these
> plots using ggplot2, but I've no clue as to how.  Has anybody
> attempted it?

A what? (google, google) Oh, interesting. Sorta like a violin plot
with really wide rug lines down the middle. There's a beanplot package
for R. No, I don't think anyone's ported it to ggplot2. Depending on
whether the beanplot package separates the computations from the
graphical code, it might not be hard to use its calculations in
combination with stat_summary to generate the plot, at least the
single-variable version.

> 2) 2nd x axis.  I understand and accept the limitation on 2nd axes as
> enforced by ggplot2, but I am curious as to whether the location of
> the x axis can be changed.  I would like to plot how concentrations of
> contaminants changes down a soil profile and it makes more sense (as
> well as commonly accepted) to have an x axis on the top rather than
> the bottom.  Can this be done?

> 3) Censored data:  How does one deal with this in ggplot2?  I've been
> using the NADA package which does a pretty good job, but I prefer the
> aesthetics of ggplot2.

What would you like ggplot2 to do? The data doesn't know it's
censored, so you have to tell ggplot to do something different. You
could use the subset option to plot the points that are at the
censoring boundaries differently somehow, perhaps using a different
geom.

-Harlan

We discovered this type of plot quite recently and like it a lot. We
find it useful to see the distribution as well as the number of
samples that cause this distribution to occur. From the description, a
bean consists of a one dimensional scatter plot, its distribution as a
density shape, and an average line for the distribution. One can do
the violin plot in ggplot2, strip plots are possible too, but the
question is how to combine the two in one. My other option is to
cheat and use the package as provided, but change the formatting to
look like a ggplot2 (because they are visually pleasing and to keep a
report looking consistent throughout). Of course, the next problem
becomes a question of how to do that. ggplot2 uses mm for font size
compared to the cex of R, for example...

That is a good question. Should have been more clear. After having a
second and third look at the documentation and "Guidelines for
computing summary statistics for data-sets containing non-detects"
2009, Huston and Juarez-Colunga, a handy pdf, I am confused as to how
approach this problem. Essentially, I am after two things:
1) Creating boxplots (okay, to be perfectly honest, beanplots, but
I'll live with the beanplots given my limitations) based on censored
data. According to their description on p. 28, a boxplot for censored
data is the same as one for uncensored data, except there is a line at
the maximum censoring limit. Easy enough to replicate, but they go
on show the limitations of substituting methods for censored data (p.
46) where they have a 0, 0.5CL, and a CL for substitutions, followed
by a "correct" boxplot. Can't figure out what method they used for
the "correct" boxplot, but I'm guessing that it uses a Kaplan-Meier or
the like to produce a plot....
2) Scatterplots where the censored data is represented visually.
Actually, not that hard to do...
